text: DistrictArea: Drakenstein (South)  · Year: 1692  · Transfer1: Original Grant from Old Cape or Old Stellenbosch Freeholds Volumes  · Transfer1Date: 12 Dec 1692  · Morgen: 60  · FarmName: Goede Hoop, De  Goede Hoop  Situated on the slopes of the Simonsberg, this farm has been referred to as Zilwermyn because of its association with the silver?mine on the mountainside above it.  Apart from the mine itself, there are ruins of a large industrial structure and a farmyard that archaeologists from Cambridge University have linked to mining operations in 1743.  The archaeologists also uncovered the foundations of the original house at Goede Hoop, situated in the back yard and at an angle to the present house.   It lies on the same axis as the stables ? possibly the oldest existing structure on the werf ? and is depicted in a sketch by S. Daniell ca 1800.  Goede Hoop was first granted to Pierre Jacob in 1688.  His widow Susanne de Vos married Nicolas Lanoy, whose own farm was to become part of Boschendal. Goede Hoop was bought by the de Villiers family in 1735 and the present homestead and cellar were built by Pieter Hendrik de Villiers.  He sold the farm in 1837 and moved to the Overberg, where he established the town of Villiersdorp.  Goede Hoop is also closely associated with Pniël, a mission station established after the abolition of slavery in 1834.  It was situated on the farm, Papiermolen, and a section of Goede Hoop, granted by Pieter Isak de Villiers and Paulus Retief who served on the board of the mission station .  Another director, J.J. Haupt, was the last owner of Goede Hoop before it was sold to Cecil John Rhodes in1897 and his name is scratched on a windowpane next to the front door.  Pieter Isak de Villiers and J.J. Haupt are buried in the graveyard at Goede Hoop, alongside unidentified graves, probably those of children and servants. The Williams family of Pniël claims descent from the de Villiers family but this is through Abraham de Villiers who was born on another farm in the valley and settled in Pniël with a local woman.  The present homestead dates from the 1820's.  The thatched roof has a leg of mutton gable and half?hipped ends.  The guttering beneath the thatch dates from the end of the 19th century and can be seen in Elliott photos. The tall sash windows with their large panes have internal shutters.  The house is partly H?shaped, with one of the back wings missing.  The south courtyard has been filled in to form a bedroom; less successful is the recent addition of a bathroom and study to the north wing.  The wine cellar occupies a dominant position on the property.  Its gable is dated 1837 and winged scrolls rest on the inside of the pilasters, a slide?slip that makes it distinctive. The building is T?shaped with a thatched roof and there is photographic evidence that the cellar windows had shutters. To the back of the building is an old flat?roof structure on the south side but on the north side is a modern garage that is not in keeping.  There are two millstones on the grounds and the cottage next to the wine cellar is thought to be the mill house.  The large house, lower down, might have been built for Paulus Retief who farmed here with Pieter Isak de Villiers.  It was occupied later by farm managers, while the General Manager of Rhodes Fruit Farms resided in the main house at "Good Hope".  During the 20th century the stables were renovated and high walls, which are now dilapidated, were built around the courtyard. The ringwalls of the property originally formed a square, extending further north than they do now and joining up with the slave quarters at the back.  This authentic row of units still has reed ceilings that have been boarded up  but are worth restoring.  *  · PropertyType: Plaas en Hofstede (Farm)  · PropertyNumber: 208  · BuyerSurname: Glodom  · BuyerName: Jan  · PurchasePriceComments: Normal Transaction  · Comments: 688  · MapCoordinates: 367351

text: DistrictArea: Drakenstein (South)  · Year: 1708  · Transfer1: Original Grant from Old Cape or Old Stellenbosch Freeholds Volumes  · Transfer1Date: 23 May 1708  · Morgen: 60  · FarmName: Goede Hoop  Goede Hoop  Situated on the slopes of the Simonsberg, this farm has been referred to as Zilwermyn because of its association with the silver?mine on the mountainside above it.  Apart from the mine itself, there are ruins of a large industrial structure and a farmyard that archaeologists from Cambridge University have linked to mining operations in 1743.  The archaeologists also uncovered the foundations of the original house at Goede Hoop, situated in the back yard and at an angle to the present house.   It lies on the same axis as the stables ? possibly the oldest existing structure on the werf ? and is depicted in a sketch by S. Daniell ca 1800.  Goede Hoop was first granted to Pierre Jacob in 1688.  His widow Susanne de Vos married Nicolas Lanoy, whose own farm was to become part of Boschendal. Goede Hoop was bought by the de Villiers family in 1735 and the present homestead and cellar were built by Pieter Hendrik de Villiers.  He sold the farm in 1837 and moved to the Overberg, where he established the town of Villiersdorp.  Goede Hoop is also closely associated with Pniël, a mission station established after the abolition of slavery in 1834. text: DistrictArea: Drakenstein (South)  · Year: 1728  · Transfer1: 1831  · Transfer1Date: 20 Apr 1728  · Transfer2: 2276  · Morgen: 60  · FarmName: Goede Hoop  Goede Hoop  Situated on the slopes of the Simonsberg, this farm has been referred to as Zilwermyn because of its association with the silver?mine on the mountainside above it.  Apart from the mine itself, there are ruins of a large industrial structure and a farmyard that archaeologists from Cambridge University have linked to mining operations in 1743.  The archaeologists also uncovered the foundations of the original house at Goede Hoop, situated in the back yard and at an angle to the present house.   It lies on the same axis as the stables ? possibly the oldest existing structure on the werf ? and is depicted in a sketch by S. Daniell ca 1800.  Goede Hoop was first granted to Pierre Jacob in 1688.  His widow Susanne de Vos married Nicolas Lanoy, whose own farm was to become part of Boschendal. Goede Hoop was bought by the de Villiers family in 1735 and the present homestead and cellar were built by Pieter Hendrik de Villiers.  He sold the farm in 1837 and moved to the Overberg, where he established the town of Villiersdorp.  Goede Hoop is also closely associated with Pniël, a mission station established after the abolition of slavery in 1834.  It was situated on the farm, Papiermolen, and a section of Goede Hoop, granted by Pieter Isak de Villiers and Paulus Retief who served on the board of the mission station .  Another director, J.J. Haupt, was the last owner of Goede Hoop before it was sold to Cecil John Rhodes in1897 and his name is scratched on a windowpane next to the front door.  Pieter Isak de Villiers and J.J. Haupt are buried in the graveyard at Goede Hoop, alongside unidentified graves, probably those of children and servants. The Williams family of Pniël claims descent from the de Villiers family but this is through Abraham de Villiers who was born on another farm in the valley and settled in Pniël with a local woman.  The present homestead dates from the 1820's.  The thatched roof has a leg of mutton gable and half?hipped ends.  The guttering beneath the thatch dates from the end of the 19th century and can be seen in Elliott photos. The tall sash windows with their large panes have internal shutters.  The house is partly H?shaped, with one of the back wings missing.  The south courtyard has been filled in to form a bedroom; less successful is the recent addition of a bathroom and study to the north wing.  The wine cellar occupies a dominant position on the property.  Its gable is dated 1837 and winged scrolls rest on the inside of the pilasters, a slide?slip that makes it distinctive. The building is T?shaped with a thatched roof and there is photographic evidence that the cellar windows had shutters. To the back of the building is an old flat?roof structure on the south side but on the north side is a modern garage that is not in keeping.  There are two millstones on the grounds and the cottage next to the wine cellar is thought to be the mill house.  The large house, lower down, might have been built for Paulus Retief who farmed here with Pieter Isak de Villiers.  It was occupied later by farm managers, while the General Manager of Rhodes Fruit Farms resided in the main house at "Good Hope".  During the 20th century the stables were renovated and high walls, which are now dilapidated, were built around the courtyard. The ringwalls of the property originally formed a square, extending further north than they do now and joining up with the slave quarters at the back.  This authentic row of units still has reed ceilings that have been boarded up  but are worth restoring.  *  · PropertyType: Plaas en Hofstede (Farm)  · PropertyNumber: 163  · SellerSurname: Hatting  · SellerName: H H  · SellerCivilStatus: Burgher  · BuyerSurname: Van Billion  · BuyerName: Bern  · BuyerCivilStatus: Burgher  · PurchasePrice: 500  · PurchasePriceComments: Normal Transaction  · SaleTerms: Mortgage  · Payments: 500  · NoofPayments: 3

DistrictArea: Drakenstein (South)  · Year: 1735  · Transfer1: 2276  · Transfer1Date: 05 Oct 1735  · Transfer2: 4471  · Morgen: 60  · FarmName: Goede Hoop  Goede Hoop  Situated on the slopes of the Simonsberg, this farm has been referred to as Zilwermyn because of its association with the silver?mine on the mountainside above it.  Apart from the mine itself, there are ruins of a large industrial structure and a farmyard that archaeologists from Cambridge University have linked to mining operations in 1743.  The archaeologists also uncovered the foundations of the original house at Goede Hoop, situated in the back yard and at an angle to the present house.   It lies on the same axis as the stables ? possibly the oldest existing structure on the werf ? and is depicted in a sketch by S. Daniell ca 1800.  Goede Hoop was first granted to Pierre Jacob in 1688.  His widow Susanne de Vos married Nicolas Lanoy, whose own farm was to become part of Boschendal. Goede Hoop was bought by the de Villiers family in 1735 and the present homestead and cellar were built by Pieter Hendrik de Villiers.  He sold the farm in 1837 and moved to the Overberg, where he established the town of Villiersdorp.  Goede Hoop is also closely associated with Pniël, a mission station established after the abolition of slavery in 1834.  It was situated on the farm, Papiermolen, and a section of Goede Hoop, granted by Pieter Isak de Villiers and Paulus Retief who served on the board of the mission station .  Another director, J.J. Haupt, was the last owner of Goede Hoop before it was sold to Cecil John Rhodes in1897 and his name is scratched on a windowpane next to the front door.  Pieter Isak de Villiers and J.J. Haupt are buried in the graveyard at Goede Hoop, alongside unidentified graves, probably those of children and servants. The Williams family of Pniël claims descent from the de Villiers family but this is through Abraham de Villiers who was born on another farm in the valley and settled in Pniël with a local woman.  The present homestead dates from the 1820's.  The thatched roof has a leg of mutton gable and half?hipped ends.  The guttering beneath the thatch dates from the end of the 19th century and can be seen in Elliott photos. The tall sash windows with their large panes have internal shutters.  The house is partly H?shaped, with one of the back wings missing.  The south courtyard has been filled in to form a bedroom; less successful is the recent addition of a bathroom and study to the north wing.  The wine cellar occupies a dominant position on the property.  Its gable is dated 1837 and winged scrolls rest on the inside of the pilasters, a slide?slip that makes it distinctive. The building is T?shaped with a thatched roof and there is photographic evidence that the cellar windows had shutters. To the back of the building is an old flat?roof structure on the south side but on the north side is a modern garage that is not in keeping.  There are two millstones on the grounds and the cottage next to the wine cellar is thought to be the mill house.  The large house, lower down, might have been built for Paulus Retief who farmed here with Pieter Isak de Villiers.  It was occupied later by farm managers, while the General Manager of Rhodes Fruit Farms resided in the main house at "Good Hope".  During the 20th century the stables were renovated and high walls, which are now dilapidated, were built around the courtyard. The ringwalls of the property originally formed a square, extending further north than they do now and joining up with the slave quarters at the back.  This authentic row of units still has reed ceilings that have been boarded up  but are worth restoring.  *  · PropertyNumber: 163  · SellerSurname: Van Billion  · SellerName: B  · SellerCivilStatus: Burgher  · BuyerSurname: De Villiers  · BuyerName: Abr  · BuyerCivilStatus: Burgher  · PurchasePrice: 1200  · PurchasePriceComments: Normal Transaction

DistrictArea: Drakenstein (South)  · Year: 1760  · Transfer1: 3535  · FarmName: Goede Hoop  Goede Hoop  Situated on the slopes of the Simonsberg, this farm has been referred to as Zilwermyn because of its association with the silver?mine on the mountainside above it.  Apart from the mine itself, there are ruins of a large industrial structure and a farmyard that archaeologists from Cambridge University have linked to mining operations in 1743.  The archaeologists also uncovered the foundations of the original house at Goede Hoop, situated in the back yard and at an angle to the present house.   It lies on the same axis as the stables ? possibly the oldest existing structure on the werf ? and is depicted in a sketch by S. Daniell ca 1800.  Goede Hoop was first granted to Pierre Jacob in 1688.  His widow Susanne de Vos married Nicolas Lanoy, whose own farm was to become part of Boschendal. Goede Hoop was bought by the de Villiers family in 1735 and the present homestead and cellar were built by Pieter Hendrik de Villiers.  He sold the farm in 1837 and moved to the Overberg, where he established the town of Villiersdorp.  Goede Hoop is also closely associated with Pniël, a mission station established after the abolition of slavery in 1834.  It was situated on the farm, Papiermolen, and a section of Goede Hoop, granted by Pieter Isak de Villiers and Paulus Retief who served on the board of the mission station .  Another director, J.J. Haupt, was the last owner of Goede Hoop before it was sold to Cecil John Rhodes in1897 and his name is scratched on a windowpane next to the front door.  Pieter Isak de Villiers and J.J. Haupt are buried in the graveyard at Goede Hoop, alongside unidentified graves, probably those of children and servants. The Williams family of Pniël claims descent from the de Villiers family but this is through Abraham de Villiers who was born on another farm in the valley and settled in Pniël with a local woman.  The present homestead dates from the 1820's.  The thatched roof has a leg of mutton gable and half?hipped ends.  The guttering beneath the thatch dates from the end of the 19th century and can be seen in Elliott photos. The tall sash windows with their large panes have internal shutters.  The house is partly H?shaped, with one of the back wings missing.  The south courtyard has been filled in to form a bedroom; less successful is the recent addition of a bathroom and study to the north wing.  The wine cellar occupies a dominant position on the property.  Its gable is dated 1837 and winged scrolls rest on the inside of the pilasters, a slide?slip that makes it distinctive. The building is T?shaped with a thatched roof and there is photographic evidence that the cellar windows had shutters. To the back of the building is an old flat?roof structure on the south side but on the north side is a modern garage that is not in keeping.  There are two millstones on the grounds and the cottage next to the wine cellar is thought to be the mill house.  The large house, lower down, might have been built for Paulus Retief who farmed here with Pieter Isak de Villiers.  It was occupied later by farm managers, while the General Manager of Rhodes Fruit Farms resided in the main house at "Good Hope".  During the 20th century the stables were renovated and high walls, which are now dilapidated, were built around the courtyard. The ringwalls of the property originally formed a square, extending further north than they do now and joining up with the slave quarters at the back.  This authentic row of units still has reed ceilings that have been boarded up  but are worth restoring.  *  · PropertyNumber: 163  · SellerSurname: Hop  · SellerName: Jan Hendrik  · SellerMaritalStatus: Widow  · SellerCivilStatus: Burgher  · BuyerSurname: Hop  · BuyerName: Christ Fred  · BuyerCivilStatus: Burgher  · PurchasePrice: 4000  · PurchasePriceComments: Normal Transaction

DistrictArea: Drakenstein (South)  · Year: 1765  · Transfer1: 4081  · Transfer2: 5404  · FarmName: Goede Hoop  Goede Hoop  Situated on the slopes of the Simonsberg, this farm has been referred to as Zilwermyn because of its association with the silver?mine on the mountainside above it.  Apart from the mine itself, there are ruins of a large industrial structure and a farmyard that archaeologists from Cambridge University have linked to mining operations in 1743.  The archaeologists also uncovered the foundations of the original house at Goede Hoop, situated in the back yard and at an angle to the present house.   It lies on the same axis as the stables ? possibly the oldest existing structure on the werf ? and is depicted in a sketch by S. Daniell ca 1800.  Goede Hoop was first granted to Pierre Jacob in 1688.  His widow Susanne de Vos married Nicolas Lanoy, whose own farm was to become part of Boschendal. Goede Hoop was bought by the de Villiers family in 1735 and the present homestead and cellar were built by Pieter Hendrik de Villiers.  He sold the farm in 1837 and moved to the Overberg, where he established the town of Villiersdorp.  Goede Hoop is also closely associated with Pniël, a mission station established after the abolition of slavery in 1834.  It was situated on the farm, Papiermolen, and a section of Goede Hoop, granted by Pieter Isak de Villiers and Paulus Retief who served on the board of the mission station .  Another director, J.J. Haupt, was the last owner of Goede Hoop before it was sold to Cecil John Rhodes in1897 and his name is scratched on a windowpane next to the front door.  Pieter Isak de Villiers and J.J. Haupt are buried in the graveyard at Goede Hoop, alongside unidentified graves, probably those of children and servants. The Williams family of Pniël claims descent from the de Villiers family but this is through Abraham de Villiers who was born on another farm in the valley and settled in Pniël with a local woman.  The present homestead dates from the 1820's.  The thatched roof has a leg of mutton gable and half?hipped ends.  The guttering beneath the thatch dates from the end of the 19th century and can be seen in Elliott photos. The tall sash windows with their large panes have internal shutters.  The house is partly H?shaped, with one of the back wings missing.  The south courtyard has been filled in to form a bedroom; less successful is the recent addition of a bathroom and study to the north wing.  The wine cellar occupies a dominant position on the property.  Its gable is dated 1837 and winged scrolls rest on the inside of the pilasters, a slide?slip that makes it distinctive. The building is T?shaped with a thatched roof and there is photographic evidence that the cellar windows had shutters. To the back of the building is an old flat?roof structure on the south side but on the north side is a modern garage that is not in keeping.  There are two millstones on the grounds and the cottage next to the wine cellar is thought to be the mill house.  The large house, lower down, might have been built for Paulus Retief who farmed here with Pieter Isak de Villiers.  It was occupied later by farm managers, while the General Manager of Rhodes Fruit Farms resided in the main house at "Good Hope".  During the 20th century the stables were renovated and high walls, which are now dilapidated, were built around the courtyard. The ringwalls of the property originally formed a square, extending further north than they do now and joining up with the slave quarters at the back.  This authentic row of units still has reed ceilings that have been boarded up  but are worth restoring.  *  · PropertyType: Plaas en Hofstede (Farm)  · PropertyNumber: 163  · SellerSurname: Russouw  · SellerName: Fred  · SellerMaritalStatus: Widow, Deceased (Seller) Widow  · BuyerSurname: Bruijns  · BuyerName: Joh  · PurchasePrice: 1900  · PurchasePriceComments: Normal Transaction

Goede HoopGoede HoopSituated on the slopes of the Simonsberg, this farm has been referred to as Zilwermyn because of its association with the silver?mine on the mountainside above it. Apart from the mine itself, there are ruins of a large industrial structure and a farmyard that archaeologists from Cambridge University have linked to mining operations in 1743. The archaeologists also uncovered the foundations of the original house at Goede Hoop, situated in the back yard and at an angle to the present house. It lies on the same axis as the stables ? possibly the oldest existing structure on the werf ? and is depicted in a sketch by S. Daniell ca 1800.Goede Hoop was first granted to Pierre Jacob in 1688. His widow Susanne de Vos married Nicolas Lanoy, whose own farm was to become part of Boschendal. Goede Hoop was bought by the de Villiers family in 1735 and the present homestead and cellar were built by Pieter Hendrik de Villiers. He sold the farm in 1837 and moved to the Overberg, where he established the town of Villiersdorp.Goede Hoop is also closely associated with Pniël, a mission station established after the abolition of slavery in 1834. It was situated on the farm, Papiermolen, and a section of Goede Hoop, granted by Pieter Isak de Villiers and Paulus Retief who served on the board of the mission station . Another director, J.J. Haupt, was the last owner of Goede Hoop before it was sold to Cecil John Rhodes in1897 and his name is scratched on a windowpane next to the front door. Pieter Isak de Villiers and J.J. Haupt are buried in the graveyard at Goede Hoop, alongside unidentified graves, probably those of children and servants. The Williams family of Pniël claims descent from the de Villiers family but this is through Abraham de Villiers who was born on another farm in the valley and settled in Pniël with a local woman.The present homestead dates from the 1820's. The thatched roof has a leg of mutton gable and half?hipped ends. The guttering beneath the thatch dates from the end of the 19th century and can be seen in Elliott photos. The tall sash windows with their large panes have internal shutters. The house is partly H?shaped, with one of the back wings missing. The south courtyard has been filled in to form a bedroom; less successful is the recent addition of a bathroom and study to the north wing.The wine cellar occupies a dominant position on the property. Its gable is dated 1837 and winged scrolls rest on the inside of the pilasters, a slide?slip that makes it distinctive. The building is T?shaped with a thatched roof and there is photographic evidence that the cellar windows had shutters. To the back of the building is an old flat?roof structure on the south side but on the north side is a modern garage that is not in keeping.There are two millstones on the grounds and the cottage next to the wine cellar is thought to be the mill house. The large house, lower down, might have been built for Paulus Retief who farmed here with Pieter Isak de Villiers. It was occupied later by farm managers, while the General Manager of Rhodes Fruit Farms resided in the main house at "Good Hope". During the 20th century the stables were renovated and high walls, which are now dilapidated, were built around the courtyard. The ringwalls of the property originally formed a square, extending further north than they do now and joining up with the slave quarters at the back. This authentic row of units still has reed ceilings that have been boarded upbut are worth restoring.*

DistrictArea: Drakenstein (South)  · Year: 1772  · Transfer1: 4471  · Morgen: 60  · FarmName: Goede Hoop  Goede Hoop  Situated on the slopes of the Simonsberg, this farm has been referred to as Zilwermyn because of its association with the silver?mine on the mountainside above it.  Apart from the mine itself, there are ruins of a large industrial structure and a farmyard that archaeologists from Cambridge University have linked to mining operations in 1743.  The archaeologists also uncovered the foundations of the original house at Goede Hoop, situated in the back yard and at an angle to the present house.   It lies on the same axis as the stables ? possibly the oldest existing structure on the werf ? and is depicted in a sketch by S. Daniell ca 1800.  Goede Hoop was first granted to Pierre Jacob in 1688.  His widow Susanne de Vos married Nicolas Lanoy, whose own farm was to become part of Boschendal. Goede Hoop was bought by the de Villiers family in 1735 and the present homestead and cellar were built by Pieter Hendrik de Villiers.  He sold the farm in 1837 and moved to the Overberg, where he established the town of Villiersdorp.  Goede Hoop is also closely associated with Pniël, a mission station established after the abolition of slavery in 1834.  It was situated on the farm, Papiermolen, and a section of Goede Hoop, granted by Pieter Isak de Villiers and Paulus Retief who served on the board of the mission station .  Another director, J.J. Haupt, was the last owner of Goede Hoop before it was sold to Cecil John Rhodes in1897 and his name is scratched on a windowpane next to the front door.  Pieter Isak de Villiers and J.J. Haupt are buried in the graveyard at Goede Hoop, alongside unidentified graves, probably those of children and servants. The Williams family of Pniël claims descent from the de Villiers family but this is through Abraham de Villiers who was born on another farm in the valley and settled in Pniël with a local woman.  The present homestead dates from the 1820's.  The thatched roof has a leg of mutton gable and half?hipped ends.  The guttering beneath the thatch dates from the end of the 19th century and can be seen in Elliott photos. The tall sash windows with their large panes have internal shutters.  The house is partly H?shaped, with one of the back wings missing.  The south courtyard has been filled in to form a bedroom; less successful is the recent addition of a bathroom and study to the north wing.  The wine cellar occupies a dominant position on the property.  Its gable is dated 1837 and winged scrolls rest on the inside of the pilasters, a slide?slip that makes it distinctive. The building is T?shaped with a thatched roof and there is photographic evidence that the cellar windows had shutters. To the back of the building is an old flat?roof structure on the south side but on the north side is a modern garage that is not in keeping.  There are two millstones on the grounds and the cottage next to the wine cellar is thought to be the mill house.  The large house, lower down, might have been built for Paulus Retief who farmed here with Pieter Isak de Villiers.  It was occupied later by farm managers, while the General Manager of Rhodes Fruit Farms resided in the main house at "Good Hope".  During the 20th century the stables were renovated and high walls, which are now dilapidated, were built around the courtyard. The ringwalls of the property originally formed a square, extending further north than they do now and joining up with the slave quarters at the back.  This authentic row of units still has reed ceilings that have been boarded up  but are worth restoring.  *  · PropertyType: Plaas en Hofstede (Farm)  · PropertyNumber: 163  · SellerSurname: De Villiers  · SellerName: Abr  · SellerMaritalStatus: Deceased (Seller) Widow  · BuyerSurname: De Villiers  · BuyerName: David Abrsz  · PurchasePrice: 9000  · PurchasePriceComments: Est
